utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Page 35 of the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Wubben. While we are at this and we have in front of us the contentious signatures and the non-contentious signatures in relation to Fejzic, when Mr. Fejzic visited you and came to your office and left you the specimen signatures and showed you the documents with his signature, did you by any chance show him the contentious, the disputed, documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I did not. My mandate was not to show anybody anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was not able even to assume what this would be used for. That's my response, Your Honours, if you'll accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Bilic. Mr. Wubben, we have roughly one hour, one hour five minutes at the moment left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'm aiming for closing within the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And please leave a little bit of time to -- for the Defence. I would imagine there isn't much of a re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not much currently, about five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Perhaps one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps one question. Roughly we are talking about ten minutes, if you could spare us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for cooperating, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Page 34, you're referring to a general visual perception of the handwriting and the signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's the first bullet, Your Honour, on page 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, this general visual perception, is that a relevant difference, Professor Bilic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can see the difference if one looks carefully at the signatures. On the left-hand side are S-1, S-2 and S-3 and, if you take a closer look, not just a superficial look, you will have an impression of these signatures, just through normal looking you can see that and you will gain an impression indicating that these are not the same signature, that these are different signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I can take it -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both from each other and -- that is what I meant by the first statement you read out. So the first step is simply to look at something closely, to perceive it and to gain an impression. That is the starting point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: If I put it to you, Professor Bilic, that these signatures are showing in general similarities, do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forger attempted to leave that impression but he was not successful. He probably had a specimen of the uncontested signature and tried to imitate it. However he was not successful in imitating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The question whether it is forgery or not, isn't that up to the Court?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I established by my investigation that there is an absolute difference between the contentious and non-contentious signatures. This signature is absolutely forged by unsuccessful imitation of a specimen of the authentic signature of this man, Hamdija Fejzic. I abide by that and Their Honours will decide and evaluate for themselves. However, as an investigator, it's up to me to state this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear enough. You still wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was simply that it was a rhetorical question by Mr. Wubben, and my submission would be that this expert certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not deciding for us, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He can certainly give testimony as to whether someone appears to have been trying to forge it or whether it was totally dissimilar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why he is here for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I mean, definitely Professor Bilic never gave the impression that he's arrogating for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Do you agree with my proposition, Professor Bilic, that the basic graphic structure of these signatures overall are referring to the same model?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assert that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wish to make this clear in my mind at least. I would like to. Which signatures are you referring to, the basic --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: All the signature, Your Honour, all the signatures on page 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are referring to the same model.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I still don't understand you. Do you agree with my proposition that the basic graphic structure of these signatures overall are referring to the same model? Which model?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: They are sharing the same model, if that's more clear, Your Honour, I would like to change my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pattern? Do you mean pattern rather than a model? Because a model is something which you are comparing to which you use to make a comparison with. So this is why the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Same structure or appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearance, all right. Appearance, pattern, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Professor Bilic, that these signatures, page 35, share the same appearance?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the contentious or the non-contentious signatures, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: All the signatures on page 35.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, by no means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In your report, page 34, Professor Bilic, you referred to the formation of the italicised Latin graphemes. That's the third bullet.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What do you mean with that statement?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refer to the way in which the writer shapes them, creates them. You can see that when you look at each of these graphemes on the contentious and uncontentious specimens, especially in the case of the grapheme z and the final č. One writer forms them in one way, and the second writer in a completely different way. It's especially characteristic that in these signatures, there is no dot on the j, and if you look at the end, the final stroke, and then if you look at the loop in the j, you see the way it is shaped and created is quite different. If you look at the initial f, it's -- on the right-hand side, it's always linked up to what follows, and it's not on the left-hand side. Then if you look, there is a curve here and a loop there. Also, the construction, this one has strokes which are superfluous, whereas the other one does not. You see, there are many more strokes on the left-hand side than there are in the signatures on the right-hand side, so the construction of the signature, its structure, is quite different. These are only the most prominent, the most glaring, differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that it can be a matter of time that these signatures showed those differences that you pointed out? I refer now to the development of a signature within the use by the same originator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, the question is, do you allow for the possibility that the difference between the contentious and the non-contentious signatures that you see on the monitor now could be attributable to the lapse of time that passed between the first set and the second set of signatures? Roughly we are talking about ten years.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By no means. This is absolutely a forged signature of Hamdija Fejzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And I don't think you're going to change that, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, if you take a look at the non-contentious signature on page 35 only, do you notice the differences between those signatures, those so-called non-contentious signatures?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only those differences which fall within the natural variation which is always there in the case of anybody's signature, yours, mine or anybody else's.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: If you take a look especial to the signatures, can you point out the differences yourself, Professor Bilic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are talking of the three signatures on the left, S-1, S-2, and S-3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, no, no the non-contentious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: N.4, N.3 and N.5 all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, can you point out any differences that you observed?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to N.4, N.3, and N.5, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Professor Bilic.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are natural variations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's not my question?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're being asked to point them out, not to comment on them. Yes, those three. The differences. Please point out to us or to Mr. Wubben the difference that you see between those three signatures, irrespective of whether they are natural variations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Or don't you notify any differences?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, yes. There are differences falling within the natural variation, but now to search for them in this way, I don't want to go into that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Why don't you want to get into that now? Don't you see them? Don't you notify them? Please tell me.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, show me these differences, if you can see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, my question is to you: Will you please show me the differences between the signatures? You're the expert.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- there are no differences at the expert level, although there may be at the visual level, which is part of the natural variation. On the expert level, as far as I'm concerned, there are no differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's his answer. I wouldn't intervene. I don't know if Mr. Jones wants to but I would suggest that he stays where he is and we move ahead. He's told you, I mean, from the professional expert point of view, he doesn't see any differences. If you want him to pinpoint the visual ones, which he attributes to a natural variation you have, of course, every right to do so and I will certainly not stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Then I will proceed on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, will you please point out the visual differences that you refer to as natural variations?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the grapheme J, the lower part, I'll show you the differences which are certainly the result of natural variation. Here. Then the final part, there is spontaneous variation in this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can you please nominate that --

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here. Also --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Professor Bilic --

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the diacritic, the placing of the diacritic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I apologise. You are pointing out indeed and I appreciate it but will you please, the second one, after the J, you pointed out a second one but you did not comment what you were pointing out. That's for the record, you see, because we could follow you by pointing out but for the record it's not --

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formation? Yes, Mr. Wubben, I understand. The formation of the lower loop, if you follow the stroke here, you can't see it up here, those are variations, but it's a grapheme written by one and the same person. And then you can observe in the initial stroke, here and here, that there is variation. It depends on how this initial stroke was started. Every signature comes into existence at a particular point in time. That's why variations exist and have to exist. If you're still interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'm still interested.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this part here, here and here, but all within the limits of variation of signatures written in a certain time sequence, in a certain place. These differences do not predominate when one makes one's final conclusions. Otherwise the conclusions would have to be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And these are all the variations, the differences, that you can point out? Or are there more, Professor Bilic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben. Probably there are more, but I showed the most striking ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did you include also, when you take a look at N.4, there is, after -- in the middle, there is something that appears to be an I and an E at the end. That's before the -- prior to the last character. Do you see? Can you point it out with your -- can you point it out, indicating --

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, there are two characters?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have that here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: These --

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it here and there, these two segments, but then we have something in the middle signature we don't have in the others. These all come under natural variation. That is why we have forensic document examination which calls for this sort of observation. We are not looking for mere similarities or dissimilarities. They have to have been created as part of a sequence of strokes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And do you also notice the difference at the last character between those three signatures?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not wish to go into these differences any more. One can see them clearly. Again, this comes under natural variation, that we have something in one signature that we don't have in the other. They are not that striking or, rather, they are irrelevant for the final conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please bear me a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I try to modify my questions in order to keep within the limit of time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Page 34, you refer in bullet number 7, the length of the signature is a relevant difference, isn't it, Professor Bilic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the signature, but it's a general difference that can be noticed quite easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But isn't it true, Professor Bilic, that the length of the signature on page 35 are broadly speaking the same?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nor can it ever be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I have a question regarding the 12th bullet on page 34. You indicated the difference of the vertical diacritic marks in small italicised letters G and T?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Does a vertical diacritic marks in C not change from dash in 1992 towards a period in 2004 or 2005? Can it be a natural variation in time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a highly personalised feature, immanent to a writer. That's why I attach so much weight to it. When you take a look at the grapheme č in the non-contentious signatures, take a look at how the diacritic icon is placed. With the contentious signatures it is not a č but a š, in Latin script. It reminds one more of a š rather than a č. You see, this is the shape of the š in Latin script, whereas here these are the dots that Mr. Wubben asked me about. When you look at this one, this one it reminds one of the grapheme š. When you look at its shape it does not really look like a č, č which comes from Fejzic. Mr. Wubben, this can be easily observed. Whereas here, there is not a single diacritic on the letter j.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But the question, Professor Bilic --

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But the question is: Doesn't the development in time of around 12 years count for that? Could it be?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would not be possible because one develops one's handwriting and signature earlier on in life and it becomes a personalised, idiosyncratic model, especially when it comes to diacritics that are placed quite automatically, rapidly and spontaneously. In no way can the lapse of time affect that. Besides, ten years earlier, he was not a child, and handwriting is something consistent for life, when a person develops one's writing style it remains there for life. There can be some slight modifications but I can, for instance, recognise my grandfather's handwriting when he was at the age of 40 as easily as when he was at the age of 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: A finalisation of the signature also pointed out as a difference, doesn't that also develop in time, let's say of around 12 years?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the case. The end part of one's signature again depends on the writer. The contentious signatures have a totally wrong ending. They do not belong to the writer. You can see that. It's very different. This end part of the signature has nothing to do with the lapse of time. Again, it is an automatic stroke. Otherwise, experts would find themselves in a lot of trouble, if they weren't able to rely on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Even given the differences between N.4, N.3, and N.5, Professor Bilic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the differences that we defined earlier, the result of spontaneous variation. We have this dotted with N.3 and N.4. N.5 it's slightly different but then again if we looked at hundreds more signatures, we would find the natural variation. Sometimes we come across the end part which is not the one that we would expect. However, there are other elements that point to the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, in N.3 and N.4, we can find other features that bring us to the conclusion that this isn't really different. This isn't something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Bilic.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will now come to the end of my questions, and I will in special now refer to the photocopies you examined. We already addressed that issue but I want to point out something via a sheet, an overview of the photocopied signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can you please put sheet number 5 on the ELMO, Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, you examined photocopies, photocopies of photocopied documents, and you commented on it. I have some questions regarding the signatures, referring to signatures S-5, S-8, S-9, S-11, S-13. Do you agree that when we take a look at S-5 and S-8, those two signatures, that it's very difficult to examine these signatures with a view to the beginning part, that it's hardly to define the beginning part of the signature that disappeared under the seal? Do you agree with that proposition, Professor Bilic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not that visible, as this is a photocopy. That's why one must place a caveat in relation to this one. I marked some of them, Mr. Wubben, because I wanted to show that some of these signatures are very different. They show a writing style unto themselves, each of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor Bilic. My question was: Do you agree or do you not agree that part of the signature is not visible, the beginning part, and that that makes it difficult to examine that part of the signature that disappeared, do you agree or not?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Do you agree or not with my proposition that the signature S-9, S-9, the -- does not show enough details that are visible?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photocopy is quite poor. One cannot really see the signature, but it is enough to see this cross line. In the middle one cannot see much but we see the ending which is quite visible, and the horizontal stroke. I marked it. One can also see how the ellipsoid of the grapheme O is formed, although we cannot see what is contained there. It being a photocopy, we can only guess what is there or not. I marked one striking feature, the dot, and the horizontal line, and then also the part where the O grapheme is formed and where it is closed and then -- let me find something else. The ending of this signature --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Professor Bilic --

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I apologise. My question is simple yes or no or I don't know. Do you agree that there are not enough details visible within this signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose for the purpose of a comparison?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: For the purpose of a comparison, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that what you had in mind, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's sufficient for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Professor Bilic, could you please answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was. Thank you, Your Honour, I'll try to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Signature S-11, do you agree or not that in that signatures, there are no details of a writing movement in the central part following the O, the first character?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can see parts of it only. Are you referring to there section here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can discern them partly. However, the impression of the stamp has covered them. But it's the ending that's quite interesting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not interested in that unless Mr. Wubben is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And doesn't the same apply for S-13?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically what it means is, is it correct that looking at S-13, you necessarily come to the conclusion that there aren't enough visible details, sufficient for a comparison? Yes or no? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were details in relation to which I gave my conclusion, which was that of most probably. That was as far as the photocopy would allow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Bilic. Now, in your report you stated that, and I quote page 17, "In principle, photocopies are not convenient for a comprehensive and serious professional expertise of handwritings, signatures, seals, seal imprints, et cetera." You also stated, "The modest results obtained through the analysis of the documents photocopied by versatile copying techniques as such do not allow for certainly and validity of results." You stated that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are going back to that. We have already defined that earlier when we were discussing photocopies, and we said the gist of this. I'd like to see that again on page 18. I don't want to reiterate what was already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Page 17, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Under 4, Your Honours, photocopies, the third line starting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So you agree that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's basically confirmed what he has already testified on that. He doesn't wish to add any more. That's what he's telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's why I just as an introduction to my following yes, asked for a yes or no, and if you can confirm that, does the quality of these copies then allow for such a strong conclusion, either positive or negative?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The quality of photocopies, in what context do you mean? I received documents that had been photocopied several times. I didn't even know how many. They had so many traces of cartridge on them that I believed them to be photocopies of photocopies of photocopies. That's why I cannot judge their quality. I cannot speak in terms of the quality of a photocopy. Depends on the photocopying machine, its quality and resolution, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, when we discussed the quality of what was visible or not on the signatures, S-5, S-8, S-9, S-11, and 13, when we discussed those, and when you agreed upon differences I pointed out -- correct me, not differences. When I pointed out lacks of what was visible or not, doesn't that mean that you are not allowed to draw such a strong conclusion, positive either or negative?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presented my conclusive finding at the level of most probably. It is for the Trial Chamber to assess that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what is being suggested to you is that the poor quality of these photocopies shouldn't have led you to come to that conclusion or that level of conclusion. This is what is being suggested by Mr. Wubben. Do you have an answer to that? Am I right, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if I'm not interpreting you well, please stop me or correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's suggesting to you that you should never have come to that sort of conclusion looking at the poor quality of these photocopies. What's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I arrived at that conclusion with great responsibility. When I saw the original contentious documents I did not take the photocopies into consideration any longer. That was my conclusion. I could have placed it as probable but that was the degree of the scale that I used, and I leave it for Their Honours to assess that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Shouldn't your conclusion, then, rather be not possible to give a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered that question. I think you better not press it any further because we will be losing time, Mr. Wubben -- precious time, I would rather say. He's answered that. He's told you. I mean, I came to that conclusion with all responsibility, that he's assuming or re-assuming.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, let's give it a number, sheet number 5 will become P622.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was wondering if number 3 was given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No they were all given exhibit number, sheet number 3 is 621. Sheet number 4 is 620. Sheet number 1 is 619.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I don't think I've made a mistake. The Prosecution case manager can correct me. I repeat, 619 is their sheet number 1. 620 is their sheet number 4. 621 is their sheet number 3, and 622 is their sheet number 5. In my record. If I have got it wrong, then I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Confirmed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, Your Honour, I was just wondering how long I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have about -- Judge Eser has got three questions so please try to limit yourself to about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Okay. That will be ample, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Professor Bilic I have just a few questions for you and most of them you can answer pretty shortly, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a suggestion that you do answer them shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, at the beginning of --

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: At the beginning of cross-examination you were asked questions about your membership of any international associations et cetera. You'll recall that. I just have two or three questions in that regard. Firstly, have you ever done analysis?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Document and handwriting analysis for international prosecutors in the state court in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about whether you had passed proficiency examinations and I believe you told us, it's just for confirmation, that in order to be a member of the commission for forensic examination of documents before the war you had to pass an official state examination as an expert; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as far as you not being a member of any international association is concerned, is it actually possible in Bosnia-Herzegovina, practising in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to be a member of an international association at present?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At present, no, although I would wish it to be so. We still have difficulties with organisation. So for the time being, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So it's nothing to do with you as an expert that you're not a member of an international association. That's true of all experts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Not even here in the Netherlands or in England or in Belgium, not all of them are members. This isn't defined that far. It is up to a person to be certified and then you have to have the institution issuing the certificate, whether it's the state court, the Supreme Court or some other institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, you also told us that you wrote instruction manuals on document examination for an institution but I'm not sure if you mentioned the institution. For which institution did you write instruction manuals?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote them for the purposes of forensic officers, how to obtain these documents or material to be examined, how to properly preserve them, and how to hand them over for analysis. I produced this official manual for the purposes of the police only. I am currently writing a manual for Judges and court staff because they lack basic knowledge from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I will ask you to keep your answers as short as possible because we want to finish very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would it be correct then when you talk about this manual being for forensic officers, that that was for the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Answer yes or no, please, Professor Bilic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And sorry that this would also require a yes or no answer because you might want to say more, but is the fact that there was a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did that have an influence on how much you were able to publish and how much were you able to develop professionally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he stated that in his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You don't have to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good. Now, if I can just ask you one thing in your report, if you go to page 5, and it's a reference to non-contentious documents by Hamdija Fejzic, and you recall being asked about this. I just want to ask you about N.3?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: N.3 is a sales contract and it's mentioned there, municipality court in Visoko. Now, is it correct or not that for the Court to certify a document like that, that in fact the person has to appear in court and prove they are who they say they are?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were asked -- I'm going to have to refer to the transcript although you may not be able to refer to this but for the rest of us it's page 29, lines 4 to 5. You were being asked about S-2, so that's a contentious sample of Hamed Salihovic. And you were asked by Mr. Wubben, "If you noticed the differences on this sheet number 1, the differences between S-2 and N.6, cannot those differences also fall within the natural variations of signatures from the same originator?" You said yes and then you went on to give an answer which was incomplete. Let me simply ask you this: Is your conclusion still or not that S-2 is probably not written by or signed by Hamed Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, you're not looking at S-2. You're looking at S.2 but you're referring to S-2 and not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, S-2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Salihovic signatures. Do we have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as far as S-2 is concerned, does your conclusion remain or not that this is probably not the signature of Hamed Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I also want to ask you, you were asked a lot of questions about the natural variation and you explained natural variation within the non-contentious sample. Did you actually -- did you find any natural variation as between the contentious samples and the non-contentious samples for Hamed Salihovic or Hamdija Fejzic or Naser Oric? Did you find differences which could be explained purely by virtue of natural variation?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all the non-contentious documents of Hamdija Fejzic, Naser Oric and Hamed Salihovic, in their non-contentious signatures.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, signatures, not documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are natural variations. This cannot be said for the contentious documents. That's quite a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, a number of -- you've been asked to look at a number of features in these different signatures during the course of cross-examination. Has what's been shown to you, asked of you, has that caused you to change any of your conclusions at all as stated in your report?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By no means. I absolutely abide by the conclusions I provided on page 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I just have one last question, I believe. I'll refer us all to page 54, lines 12 to 13 of the transcript. I'll read it for you Professor Bilic, and it refers to the signatures of Hamdija Fejzic. And you said, and this is perhaps a general remark, you said, "And then you can observe in the initial stroke here and here that there is variation. It depends on how this initial stroke was started." I want to ask you something about that, about how someone starts a stroke. Now, as far as Hamdija Fejzic is concerned, did you in fact see how he started his stroke and how he performed his signature physically because he did it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did see that, and it was extremely important to me. You have observed this very well, yes. I did pay attention to that when he was writing in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Judge Brydensholt hasn't got any questions. Judge Eser?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just a question that came up since you have been asked with regard to membership of national organisations and other organisations, because you gave a very global statement when you told us that you were no member of an international organisation or association, did you only have official organisations in mind or did it also apply to any private societies or organisations or associations?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to official associations and organisations. In my country, we have two professional associations. In Republika Srpska and in the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm a member of both. But we don't have anything else yet. I would like to be a member of an international organisation, but I don't know how. I have a lot of knowledge and experience and I would like to cooperate with colleagues from other countries in my field of expertise. There are associations of private experts in Great Britain and the USA. Depends on the country. Differs from country to country. I haven't gone into how they register themselves or -- but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: My main question I have is the following: When it comes to the non-contentious documents with regard to Hamed Salihovic, you had listed on pages 3, 4, in total, 14 documents, but if I look to the map, which is on pages -- what is it? Page 26 to 28, I only find seven signatures of non-contentious signatures. Is there a reason why you only gave seven signatures out of 14, which -- documents which are listed?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will respond. Had I put there all 14 signatures there, it would have been overcrowded, so I made a selection. Had I included more signatures, it would have been perhaps overcrowded. I simply selected at random from the entire map these signatures. This does not mean I did not analyse the other signatures, but to make the map easier to look at and understand, I didn't include them all in it. I chose these at random. And I think I have the right to do that as an investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: When it comes to Hamdija Fejzic, you listed there 12 documents -- I mean four and five with different signatures, and I only find three documents that are listed. Is there a reason? Would it be a problem of overcrowding, I guess?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle was the same. There are only three contentious ones. I would have had to reduce them in size, but the principle of selection was the same. All the non-contentious signatures were looked at and I put these in the map for purposes of illustration. The map is not meant to include every signature that was looked at. This is a selection which, in my view, helps one to visualise and observe what is relevant and on the basis of what the conclusions were made. That's my method of work. Sometimes you can have more than 50 non-contentious documents but if all of them were included in a map it would be overcrowded. The purpose of the map -- I think I've tried to explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. Now if you would like me to ask you to compare the signatures of Naser Oric and the signatures of Hamed Salihovic, and from a visual appearance, from a visual appearance, would you agree that the differences with regard to Naser Oric's signatures are not as great as the differences with regard to the Salihovic signatures? If you look at them at first appearances with regard to Salihovic, the differences appear a little greater than with regard to Naser Oric? Is that a correct impression of mine?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a correct impression, Your Honour, and you have this impression because the contentious signature has more strokes. It appears larger. It creates more of an effect, as compared to the writing in the contentious signatures of Naser Oric, which visually appear shorter, with fewer strokes. Your impression is correct and this shows that you have noticed what I wanted you to notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask a question arising out of the questions asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's only one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Eser was asking a moment ago about impressions, about his impression that there was a greater difference in the Oric signatures and you said "Yes, visually there is that appearance because there are fewer strokes." In fact, is there a greater real difference between the Oric contentious signatures and the non-contentious than between the Salihovic ones or a lesser difference? Can you just comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: ESAD BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will comment on it. There is a far greater difference between the contentious signatures of Oric than in the case of the contentious signatures of Hamdija Fejzic. One can see that by simple visual observation of the maps. His Honour Judge Eser has pointed that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He mentioned Fejzic but I think it was Salihovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Salihovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to Fejzic or Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Salihovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I wanted to compare Salihovic and Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can put the question one last time. I can make it nice and clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is there actually any greater difference between the contentious Salihovic signatures and the non-contentious Salihovic signatures than there is between the non-contentious Oric and the contentious Oric signatures? That's the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, you are limited only to the visual aspect, because that was Judge Eser's -- Judge Eser was limiting himself to the visual appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm concerned whether the visual appearance actually amounts to a real difference in expert terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: That was not my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Never entertained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As long as that is understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Professor Bilic, I can't tell you how happy I am that we've made it in time to send you back home and not keep you here waiting any longer. I think I need to thank you, Mr. Wubben, first and foremost for having cooperated so much today but, of course, also to the Defence team. Together we have been able to manage this. You will receive all the assistance you require, Professor Bilic, to facilitate your return back home, and our usher will accompany you out -- escort you out of the courtroom. On behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, myself, and also on behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over, and last but not least wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So before we wind up, in -- during the sitting, I sent a message to the Defence to more or less get a feedback as to whether definitively we will be hearing the evidence of Colonel whatever his name is, I know his name but I prefer not to mention it. Yes, I know it. I'm avoiding mentioning it. On Wednesday, as suggested. The idea that I get back from the Defence is that they will be able to confirm later on, possibly tomorrow. But that the indications are still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, there are knows indications and we will communicate with your legal officer tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In the meantime I have signed also, before coming in for the second session, the Mauzer thing, the Mauzer motion, in line with your prior statement and making it operative until Monday. In other words, you're expected to deliver. And we will, of course, be working on the rest this weekend, anxiously waiting for the various responses due Tuesday. All right? Thank you. I wish you all a happy weekend. And I understand you will be going to Berlin to authenticate the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that is being taken care of as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
